AD.ACCOUNT.STALE_ENABLED.title: Accounts nobody uses are still switched on
AD.ACCOUNT.STALE_ENABLED.whyItMatters: Every enabled account is a door into the network. Accounts belonging to people who left, or service accounts nobody maintains any more, are rarely monitored and their passwords are rarely changed, so an attacker who guesses or steals one is unlikely to be noticed.
whatToDo: Confirm with the account owner or their manager whether each account is still needed.
Disable the accounts that are no longer needed, and move them to a dedicated organizational unit so they are easy to review later.
Delete them after a retention period that suits your organization, typically 30 to 90 days after disabling.
For service accounts that must stay, document the owner and set a password rotation schedule.

references.label: Microsoft: Active Directory Domain Services documentation

AD.POLICY.WEAK_PASSWORD.title: The domain password rules are easy to defeat
AD.POLICY.WEAK_PASSWORD.whyItMatters: The domain password policy sets the floor for every account in the domain. Short passwords can be cracked offline in a short time once an attacker obtains a password hash, and with no lockout threshold an attacker can keep guessing passwords over the network without ever being locked out.
whatToDo: Raise the minimum password length to at least 14 characters in the Default Domain Policy.
Turn password complexity back on, or replace it with a longer minimum length plus a banned password list.
Set an account lockout threshold so repeated failed sign-ins are stopped, and pair it with a lockout duration your help desk can live with.
Test the change on a small group first, because raising these settings affects every user at their next password change.

references.label: Microsoft: Active Directory Domain Services documentation

AD.PRIVILEGE.EXCESSIVE_ADMIN_MEMBERSHIP.title: Too many people have full control of the domain
AD.PRIVILEGE.EXCESSIVE_ADMIN_MEMBERSHIP.whyItMatters: Members of Domain Admins can do anything in the domain, including reading every password hash. Each extra member is another account an attacker can target to take over the whole environment, and nested groups make this worse because the real member count is larger than the group appears to hold.
whatToDo: List everyone who is currently a member, including members inherited through nested groups, and confirm each one still needs that level of access.
Remove day to day user accounts from privileged groups. Give administrators a separate admin account used only for administrative work.
Avoid nesting ordinary groups such as help desk groups inside privileged groups, because it hides the true membership.
Review the membership on a fixed schedule, for example once a quarter.

references.label: Detecting and mitigating Active Directory compromises (joint advisory)

AD.PRIVILEGE.UNCONSTRAINED_DELEGATION.title: Some computers can impersonate any user who connects to them
AD.PRIVILEGE.UNCONSTRAINED_DELEGATION.whyItMatters: A computer trusted for unconstrained delegation keeps a copy of the Kerberos ticket of everyone who connects to it. If an attacker controls that computer and a domain administrator connects to it, the attacker can reuse that ticket and take over the domain.
whatToDo: Identify why delegation was configured and whether the service still needs it.
Replace unconstrained delegation with constrained delegation limited to the specific services required.
Mark administrative accounts as sensitive and not allowed to be delegated.

AD.PRIVILEGE.KERBEROASTING.title: Service accounts whose passwords can be cracked offline
AD.PRIVILEGE.KERBEROASTING.whyItMatters: These accounts run services, so they are registered in the directory under a service name. Active Directory is designed to hand any signed-in user a ticket for a registered service, and that ticket is locked with the service account's own password. An attacker with any ordinary account, even a brand new one, can therefore collect those tickets and then try to guess the passwords on their own computer, where no lockout stops them and nothing in your logs looks unusual. The whole attack needs no special permission at all. If one of these accounts is also an administrator, cracking its password hands over the entire domain.
whatToDo: Give each of these accounts a long random password, 25 characters or more. Length is what defeats offline guessing, and nobody has to type a service account password by hand.
Remove any of these accounts from Domain Admins and other administrative groups. A service almost never needs domain-wide rights, and those are the accounts worth the attacker's time.

Set the account to use AES encryption only, by ticking the two AES options under the account's Delegation or Account tab. Accounts left on the default still accept the older RC4 encryption, which is far quicker to crack.
Where the service supports it, replace the account with a group managed service account. The directory then generates and rotates the password itself and this problem goes away.
Remove the service name registration from any account that no longer runs a service.
